com.prism3.description: Which glyph, from the set's own list of names, so an unknown name fails at compile time instead of rendering as an invisible gap. The list (IconName) is generated from the icon set, so a new glyph reaches the API the day it joins the set. A code projection that widens the type back to a plain string loses that check. Per-glyph components, such as IconSearch, are the equivalent for a tree-shaken delivery.

Snaps to the pixel grid: 16, 20, 24 or 32px. Arbitrary sizes are refused, because off-grid scaling blurs strokes between hardware pixels. The size words match every other component; the pixel values come from the icon size tokens.

Ink. Defaults to inherit (currentColor), so the glyph follows its host's hover, disabled and error colors with no script. A semantic value pins it instead, so an error glyph keeps its color where the inherited one would make it invisible. Raw hex is not accepted, so contrast is enforced centrally rather than at each call site.

The only route to an accessible name. With a label the glyph is meaningful: role="img" and aria-label. Without one it is decorative: aria-hidden="true". That is the default and usually the correct answer, because a named icon beside its own text announces twice ("Email, Email"). Inside an icon-only control the control carries the name and this stays empty; never name both.

Which mark, as kind and provider: payment/visa, logo/apple-pay, button/paypal-gold, provider/google, social/instagram-mono. The list is generated from the mark set, so an unknown name fails at compile time, and a provider added to the set reaches the list the day it lands.
The height: 20, 24 or 32px, from the icon size tokens. The width follows from the mark's own proportion, so a payment tile stays 8 by 5 and a logo keeps its width.

The accessible name, when the mark carries information the page states nowhere else, as in a row of accepted cards: the mark then has role="img" and aria-label. Without a label it is decorative and hidden from assistive tech, which is right inside a button or link whose own text or label names the provider.

The ground the ring is drawn against. default for a normal surface; inverse for a dark or brand-filled one, where the default ring would sit on a similar hue and lose its 3:1 separation. A host that cannot know its ground picks default; a host with its own surface option passes it through (see Button), so the ring on a dark band is the inverse ring.

How far outside the host the ring sits. control is the standard gap of about 2px; field is 0, because an input's own border already supplies the separation and a gap there reads as a double border. Two values, one for each offset token (focus.ring.offset and focus.ring.offset-field).
Visible label; verb-first, sentence case, ≤3 words. Always required here — an icon-only control is the separate icon-button, which requires an accessible name instead.
Action handler. Suppressed while isPending or isInactive.

Visual treatment over the color, decoupled from intent so the matrix scales by addition. filled = interactive fill + on-fill ink; outline = border + text ink; text = ink only. (Reconciled from solid/outline/plain.)
Control size — drives height, padding, and label type.

The ground the button sits on. default for a normal page; inverse for a dark or brand-filled band, where the button binds its color.inverse counterparts so fill, ink, border, overlay and the disabled treatment keep contrast against the flipped surface. A host that cannot know its ground picks default, and the designer sets inverse on the instance — the same answer the nested focus ring gives.

Text appearance only. flush removes the inline padding on both sides, so the label lines up with the content edge above and below it, whether the button starts, ends or centers a row. A flush button hovers by color only, and its hit target keeps its height.
Stretch to container. Aliases: block / isFullWidth.
Opinionated default 'button' to neutralize the platform's submit-on-enter-in-form trap; require 'submit' explicitly.
Delays the spinner, preserves width, keeps focus (aria-disabled, not native disabled), suppresses re-fire, announces busy. Preferred over a loading prop.
Focusable disabled — visually muted, retains tab order, surfaces the blockage reason on focus. Use for a control blocked by satisfiable app state (e.g. submit on an incomplete form).
Native disabled. Reserved for controls fundamentally irrelevant to the current view; removes from tab order + a11y tree. Prefer isInactive for anything relevant-but-blocked.
Icon / avatar / counter / spinner before the label.
Icon / caret / indicator after the label.

A destination, for a navigation that needs a button's weight, such as "Continue to checkout". With an href, the button renders an <a href> in the same style, Enter follows it, and type and disabled no longer apply. Anything lighter is a Link.

Extends the visible label with context it does not carry ("Delete invoice 1042" on a "Delete" button). Start it with the visible text, so a voice-control user who speaks the label still activates the control (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name).

Which wallet. Each needs its provider's script on the page, which draws the button.

The provider's color style, from its own list, passed to the provider: Apple Pay black, white, white-outline; Google Pay black, white; PayPal gold, blue, silver, white, black; Shop Pay purple. Pick it for the ground the button sits on: dark buttons on light grounds, light ones on dark grounds. any passes no style, so the provider draws its default. A style the provider does not offer is refused.
The height: 36, 44 or 56px. Google Pay and Shop Pay have no small size and PayPal no large one, because each provider sets a smallest and a largest height.

The provider's wording, from its own list, passed to the provider: plain shows the logo alone; buy, checkout, donate, order, pay and subscribe add the provider's words, translated by the provider. A value the provider does not offer falls back to plain.
Which account the button signs in with. The button calls that provider's own sign-in, which needs the provider's script on the page.

The provider's color style, from its own list: Apple black, white, outline; Google light, dark, neutral; Facebook blue, white. Unset, the first in the provider's list. A style another provider uses is refused.
The height: 36, 44 or 56px. Give every sign-in button in a group the same size.

The provider's wording, from its own list, translated by the app: Apple continue, sign-in, sign-up; Google continue, sign-in, sign-up; Facebook continue, login. The provider's name is never translated. A wording the provider does not offer is refused.
Fill the column instead of hugging the label. The button never drops under 140px wide.
Called before the provider's sign-in starts, for analytics or a loading state. The sign-in itself is the provider's.

Default ghost — icon-only actions usually sit in toolbars, not as filled calls to action. The third appearance is ghost (a borderless, fill-less icon action) because an icon-only control has no text; Button keeps text. Emphasis is the appearance axis; the color is the component (IconButton / IconButton.Destructive / IconButton.Neutral).
Square control; height drives both dimensions.

The corner silhouette, and geometry only. square is the button's normal rounded rectangle (radius.md); circular is full-round (radius.round), the tap target read as a disc. No color, state, or token difference between the two — only the corner radius — which is why it is a 2-value option and not a separate component (each intent, by contrast, binds its own interactive color family). Both stay square in dimension (height drives width); shape rounds the corners, it does not change the box.
