The label text — a noun phrase, sentence case, ≤3 words, no trailing colon ("Email address", not "Enter your email address here").
The id of the field it names — a native <label for>. Set by the host when composed inside a field component (useId).

Whether the field is required. On shows the marker beside the label; off, the default, hides it, and the host's own required prop defaults off too. Never the sole signal: the field also carries required / aria-required, so the state is not marker-only.

Three steps. Scales the type (type.body.xs, sm and md: 12, 14 and 16px), not padding alone, one body step below the input of the same field size. Every field host passes its own size through, so a small field nests the small label. small, the default, is the 12px label.

The label's ink. primary, the default, is the full-strength ink every field host nests: the label leads, and the placeholder below it is the quieter hint. secondary is the de-emphasized ink, for a label that should step back. Semantic roles, never shades (color.text.primary and color.text.secondary), so a brand that changes its text palette carries the label with it.

How heavy the label reads. These are intents, not role names: regular resolves the brand's default body weight, bold the heaviest body weight the brand ships — Bold (700) on a brand that ships it, Medium (500) where that is its heaviest body cut. Use it for a label that has to carry a section, not for emphasis inside a form — a form where every label is bold has no emphasis in it.
default = helper guidance (neutral); error / warning / success = a validation result. The status re-points both the caption ink and the icon at the matching semantic role.
The message text. For error status, say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3) — "Enter a valid email, e.g. name@example.com", not "Invalid input".

Overrides the leading status glyph, aria-hidden (the text carries the meaning). Rarely needed: each validation status already picks its own mark — an exclamation in a triangle for error, in a circle for warning, a circled check for success — so this is for a host with a domain-specific status mark, not for supplying the one the status implies. On the default status there is no glyph unless one is supplied here, which is what makes it the only status where this prop adds a node rather than replacing one.
Set by the host so it can reference this node from the field's aria-describedby chain. Auto-generated with useId when composed inside TextField.
The visible, persistent label (rendered as FieldLabel). Required — a visually-hidden label is the only label-less case, and it still exists in the DOM. Never the placeholder.
Controlled value; pair with onChange. A controlled value with no onChange is read-only by accident.
Uncontrolled initial value — preferred for form-library ergonomics.
Change handler (also onBlur / onFocus).
Attribute-only variants (mobile keyboard + autofill). Not number: numeric input needs a number field (not built yet). search / password are better served by their thin specializations.
An example only ("name@example.com"); vanishes on input; nothing load-bearing lives here.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage, default status); wired via aria-describedby. Show the format before failure.

The validation state. Each non-default status swaps the input border to its own boundary (border-only — error → danger, warning → warning, success → success) and sets the nested message to the matching status; default is neutral. error also sets aria-invalid. The values align with FieldMessage's status axis, so this drives the nested message directly.
The validation text shown at error / warning / success, added to aria-describedby. For error, say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3), never "Invalid".

Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message below the input. Never hides a message the field needs: turn it on wherever there is helper or validation text.
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker.
Native disabled — removed from tab order, not submitted, silent to assistive tech, contrast-exempt. Reserve for fields irrelevant in the current state.

Distinct from disabled: focusable, selectable and copyable, submitted with the form, and passes contrast. Use for a value the user may read/copy but not edit (a generated key). The component's live edge.
Satisfies SC 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose — an accessibility obligation, not a convenience.
Selects the mobile virtual keyboard.

A leading text affix inside the field, before the value — a currency symbol or a unit ("$", "€"). Not part of the value and aria-hidden, so the label or helper text carries what it means. Follows the locale's placement (a symbol before or after the number). A glyph is leadingIcon, not this.

A trailing text affix inside the field, after the value — a unit or a domain ("kg", ".com"). Not part of the value and aria-hidden, so the label or helper text carries what it means. A glyph or a clear / reveal action is trailingIcon / clearable, not this.

An optional leading glyph before the value (a purpose or category mark, such as search), aria-hidden and never the accessible name. Hidden by default; the file nominates the swap target. Signals the field's purpose; validation never mutates it.

An optional trailing glyph at the field's trailing edge — a decorative mark (aria-hidden), or the glyph of a clear / reveal action, which in code is a focusable button with its own accessible name. The decorative-vs-interactive split is load-bearing. As a button, its hit area is at least 24×24 px, drawn around the 20px glyph, and adds no height to the field. Hidden by default; the file nominates the swap target.
Adds a labeled Clear button that announces the cleared state and returns focus to the input (the recurring trap is stranding focus).
Async validation/value — a spinner replaces an adornment without reflow; sets aria-busy; does not block typing unless intended.

Three tiers that scale the input type with the field (small 14px, medium 16px, large 18px, from type.body.sm, md and lg), the nested label one step below it (12 / 14 / 16), and the padding. Every size keeps the 44px target: small is smaller type and padding, not a smaller target; large is taller. small is for fine pointers only: on a coarse pointer (@media (pointer: coarse)) the code sets the small input to 16px, because iOS Safari zooms the page when it focuses an input under 16px. The field's edge, outline or underline, is the brand's Field style setting, not a prop.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted, tying label→input and the aria-describedby chain.
A real <input name> so the field works uncontrolled, in a native <form>, with useFormStatus / Server Actions, and the Constraint Validation API.

The visible, persistent label (rendered as FieldLabel). Required — a visually-hidden label is the only label-less case, and it still exists in the DOM. Never the placeholder. The same prop as TextField's.
Controlled value; pair with onChange. The same prop as TextField's.
Change handler (also onBlur / onFocus). The same prop as TextField's.
An example only; vanishes on input; nothing load-bearing lives here. The same prop as TextField's.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage, default status); wired via aria-describedby. Show the format and any length limit before failure. The same prop as TextField's.
Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message below the field. The same prop as TextField's. Never hides a message the field needs.

Initial and minimum height, in lines not pixels — a line count recomputes against the current line-height when the user raises their font size, where a pixel floor does not. Also a content cue: two rows signals brevity, six signals "write more". cols is dead on the web; width comes from CSS.

The sizing model in one prop, so two props cannot contradict each other. vertical (the drag handle) for standalone form fields; auto (grow within minRows/maxRows) for composers; none where layout stability wins. Never horizontal or both — altering the inline dimension shatters grid and flex layouts for no user gain.
Auto-grow floor, in lines. Only meaningful with resize="auto".

Auto-grow cap, in lines; beyond it the field scrolls. Always set this when auto-growing — an uncapped field pushes the submit button off-screen on a long paste, which is a shipped failure in the field, not a hypothetical.

Character limit, counted by grapheme (Intl.Segmenter) rather than UTF-16 code unit — a flag emoji costs 4 units and a ZWJ family up to 11, so a .length limit hits non-Latin and emoji users artificially early. Enforce soft: allow the overflow, set aria-invalid, show the counter in error, block submit. Never the native hard maxlength, which silently truncates pasted overflow with no signal to anyone, at users included.
The character counter — first-class here, unlike on TextField. Only ever with a real limit: a counter on an unlimited field implies a cap that does not exist.
Native passthrough; worth surfacing because structured input often wants it off.

Composer opt-in: Enter submits, Shift+Enter inserts a newline. Not the base default — Enter inserting a newline is the platform contract a multi-line field advertises via aria-multiline, and hijacking it silently can lose a screen-reader user a drafted message. Whenever true, pair it with a real visible submit button and a visible "Shift+Enter for a new line" hint (SC 3.3.2). A composer that submits on Enter by default is its own specialization, named MessageComposer or ChatInput, not this base field.

The validation state. Each non-default status swaps the field border to its own boundary (border-only — error → danger, warning → warning, success → success) and sets the composed message to the matching status; default is neutral. error also sets aria-invalid. The same prop, with the same values, as TextField and Select.

The validation text shown at error / warning / success, added to aria-describedby. For error, say what is wrong and how to fix it, with the number when it is a length limit (SC 3.3.3), never "Invalid".
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker. The same prop as TextField's.
Native disabled — removed from tab order, not submitted, silent to assistive tech, contrast-exempt. Reserve for fields irrelevant in the current state. The same prop as TextField's.

Distinct from disabled: focusable, selectable and copyable, submitted with the form, and passes contrast. Use for text the user may read or copy but not edit (a submitted message, a generated summary). The same prop as TextField's.
Content arriving asynchronously, such as a draft streaming into the field: sets aria-busy; does not block typing unless intended. The same prop as TextField's.

Scales the value type with the field (small 14px, medium 16px, large 18px, from type.body.sm, md and lg), the nested label one step below it (12 / 14 / 16), and the padding. Not the height: that belongs to rows / auto-grow, so the reserved rows grow with the type's line height. small is for fine pointers only: on a coarse pointer (@media (pointer: coarse)) the code sets the small textarea to 16px, because iOS Safari zooms the page when it focuses a field under 16px. The same prop, with the same values, as TextField and Select.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted, tying label→textarea and the aria-describedby chain. The same prop as TextField's.
A real <textarea name> so the field works uncontrolled, in a native <form>, with useFormStatus / Server Actions, and the Constraint Validation API. The same prop as TextField's.
The filled/checked appearance. Driven by the host row from the group's value array — a bare Checkbox.Control is styled by the coordinate, not wired to state here.
The mixed appearance — the dash glyph. Presentational, for parent/child select-all hierarchy, never a third value a user clicks to; the host carries aria-checked="mixed".
Scales the control square (both axes from one key, square by construction), its corner and its glyph. The host row passes its own size through by follow, so the nested control tracks the row.
The disabled skin — a contrast-exempt fill/border/glyph treatment. Set on the host, followed here.
The validation status. error draws the danger border on the box at every interaction state; default is neutral. Set by the host row, or by the group around it, and followed here.
Required only for a genuinely standalone control with no host row to name it — the Row provides the accessible name through the label, so a nested control must not double-label.

The controlled binary. Pair with onChange; use defaultChecked for the uncontrolled form. Named for the DOM attribute rather than the framework idiom — checked, not isChecked/isSelected. Inside a Checkbox.Group this is derived from the group's value array and a consumer should not also wire it here.
Uncontrolled initial value. Never true for a consent checkbox — pre-checked consent is a dark pattern and, for marketing consent, often unlawful.

The mixed visual state — dash glyph, aria-checked="mixed". Presentational: the underlying value is still true/false, and this is for parent/child select-all hierarchy only, never a third state a user can click to. There is no indeterminate HTML attribute — it is a DOM property (node.indeterminate = true), which is the single most common checkbox bug; in React apply it through a synchronous ref callback rather than a JSX prop.

Rich content: a node, not a string. The substrate's label is a string above the field; this one sits inline-end, doubles as the hit target, and must be able to hold a link, because the single most common real checkbox label is a consent line with one in it ("I agree to the Terms of Service"). A standalone control with no label is checkbox-control, which then requires an external aria-label/aria-labelledby.
Optional helper beneath the label, describedby-wired — the detail that qualifies the choice without lengthening the label.
Restated rather than inherited: the substrate's change yields a string, this one yields the resulting boolean alongside the event.

The string submitted when checked (the platform default is "on"), and the element this row contributes to a Checkbox.Group's array. An unchecked box submits nothing at all rather than a false value — the missing-key trap.

Native disabled: removed from the tab order, not submitted, contrast-exempt. Disables the whole row: the nested control takes its disabled skin and the label dims. Reserve for an option that does not apply in the current state.

Restated only for the caveat: <input type="checkbox"> has no working readonly — only disabled — so a genuinely read-only checkbox needs aria-readonly plus a prevented toggle, or is better rendered as static text. Decide which explicitly; the default of doing neither is a control that looks interactive and silently is not.

The validation status of a standalone checkbox — a consent line that must be checked. error draws the danger border on the box and sets aria-invalid; pair it with an error message the host shows. Inside a Checkbox.Group the group sets this on every row; never set it on one row of a group.

Scales the control square, the label's type ramp, the box↔label gap and the row's minimum height. The square reads control.size.<rung>.height on both axes — square by construction rather than by two tokens agreeing — and not icon.size.*, which is 16/20/24 in every brand the engine ships and so would hold a control rigid that should move with brand density.

The group heading, rendered as the nested FieldLabel and the group's accessible name (role="group" + aria-labelledby). Names the decision the set answers ("Notification preferences"), letting its rows read the abstracted-up short labels ("Email", "SMS", "Push").
The options, each a Checkbox.Row, in order. Three by default; a designer adds, removes and reorders them in place.

The controlled array of checked option values. The group owns it; each row's checked appearance is derived (checked = value.includes(row.value)), never wired on the row. Pair with onChange; use defaultValue for the uncontrolled form.
Uncontrolled initial selection. Never pre-check a consent option — a dark pattern, and for marketing consent often unlawful.
Fires with the new value array when any row toggles. The group dispatches it; a row never owns its own onChange inside a group.

Whether at least one option must be chosen. Off by default. Drives the nested FieldLabel's required marker and aria-required on the group. Group-level: an individual row never owns its own required. A form that marks the optional minority instead sets this false.
Scales the group — the label's type and every row (control square, label ramp, gap) together, passed into the nested FieldLabel and rows by follow, so the group scales with the rest of the form.
A shared control name so the set submits as one field and works uncontrolled in a native form.

The group's validation status. error passes to every row, which draws the danger border on each box, shows validationMessage under the options, and sets aria-invalid on the group. default is neutral. Set it here, never on one row.
The error text shown under the options at error, added to the group's aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3): "Select at least one option", never "Invalid".
Disables the whole set — every row and the label dim, driven by the group's context (the field's native disabled is the source of truth). The group has no disabled treatment of its own.

The selected appearance — the inner dot present. Driven by the host row from the group's scalar value — a bare Radio.Control is styled by the coordinate, not wired to state here, and never holds a boolean of its own (selection is group.value === option.value).

Scales the control circle (both axes from one key, round by construction) and the inner dot. Both read control.size.*, which moves a rung with brand density; icon.size.* would resolve and measure the wrong thing (the glyph artboard ladder). The host row passes its own size through by follow, so the nested control tracks the row.
The disabled skin — a contrast-exempt border/dot treatment. Set on the host, followed here.
The validation status, set by the Radio group and never by one radio alone: the group passes it to every option, so error draws the danger ring on all of them at once. default is neutral.
Required only for a genuinely standalone control with no host row to name it — the Row provides the accessible name, so a nested control must not double-label.

Required, where Checkbox.Row's is optional. This is the option's identity within its group, not a string that happens to be submitted. Selection is derived from it: checked = (group.value === props.value). The option never holds a boolean of its own.

Rich content, inline-end of the control, and part of the hit target — the Checkbox.Row label model, inherited. Option labels are parallel, mutually exclusive and brief: the same grammatical shape across the set, with no overlap that would make two options both apply. Long labels wrap rather than truncate, with the control centered within the first line-box so it stays on the first line. Per-option detail or price belongs in description, not in the label.
Per-option helper beneath the label, describedby-wired. This is where the detail that makes an option distinguishable goes — the price, the delivery estimate, the caveat.
Set by the Radio group, never by one radio alone: the group passes its validation status to every option, and error draws the danger ring on each. A consumer sets validation on the group, not here.

Native disabled: removed from the tab order, not submitted, contrast-exempt. Disables the whole row: the nested control takes its disabled skin and the label dims. Reserve for an option that does not apply in the current state.

Restated for the caveat Checkbox.Row carries: <input type="radio"> has no working readonly, only disabled, so a genuinely read-only option needs aria-readonly plus a prevented change, or is better rendered as static text. Usually set on every option of a group at once. Decide which explicitly; the default of doing neither is a control that looks interactive and silently is not.
Scales the row — the control-to-label gap, the row's minimum height, the label's type — and is passed through to the nested Radio.Control by follow, scaling the circle's diameter and the inner dot's.

The group heading, rendered as the nested FieldLabel and the group's accessible name (role="radiogroup" + aria-labelledby). Names the decision the set answers ("Shipping method", "How should we contact you?"), letting its rows read the abstracted-up short labels ("Standard", "Express", "Overnight"). Mandatory for meaning: without it assistive tech announces an orphaned "radio button, 1 of 3" with no indication of what is being chosen.
The options, each a Radio.Row, in order. Three by default; a designer adds, removes and reorders them in place.

The controlled scalar selected option value — exactly one, where Checkbox.Group owns an array. The group owns it; each row's checked appearance is derived (checked = (value === row.value)), never wired on the row. Pair with onChange; use defaultValue for the uncontrolled form.

Uncontrolled initial selection — a single option value. Start empty (unset) to force a deliberate choice; pre-select only where a genuinely safe recommended default exists, and never pre-select a consent-shaped option.

Fires with the new scalar value when a different row is selected. The group dispatches it; a row never owns its own onChange inside a group. Keep it cheap — selection follows focus by default, so a screen-reader user arrowing through fires it at every step.

Whether an option must be chosen. Off by default. Drives the nested FieldLabel's required marker and aria-required on the group. Group-level: an individual row never owns its own required. An optional group must instead carry an explicit "None" option, because a radio cannot be deselected — a stray click is otherwise permanent.
Scales the group — the label's type and every row (control circle, label ramp, gap) together, passed into the nested FieldLabel and rows by follow, so the group scales with the rest of the form.

The shared control name — load-bearing here, not a submission convenience: it is what enforces browser-level exclusivity across the set, so every group sets one. An individual option never sets its own, which would break exclusivity outright.

The group's validation status. error passes to every option, which draws the danger ring on each, shows validationMessage under the options, and sets aria-invalid on the group. default is neutral. A radio is never invalid on its own, so this is the only place to set it.
The error text shown under the options at error, added to the group's aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3): "Select a shipping method", never "Invalid".
Disables the whole set — every row and the label dim, driven by the group's context (the native disabled is the source of truth). The group has no disabled treatment of its own.

The on/off appearance. Driven by the host row — a bare Switch.Control is styled by the coordinate, not wired to state here. The flip is immediate by the Row's contract; this atom only renders the two positions.

The X/checkmark-in-the-thumb affordance — a check when on, an X when off, a cue beyond track color and thumb position. On by default; turn it off where the thumb position and track color are enough. Never the sole state signal — thumb position carries the state. Not hardcoded "On"/"Off" text, which is rejected outright.

Two rungs, not three: switches rarely warrant a large. Scales the track's height and length and the thumb's diameter. All read control.size.*, which moves a rung with brand density; icon.size.* would measure the wrong thing. The host row passes its own size through by follow.
The disabled skin — a contrast-exempt fill/border/thumb treatment. Set on the host, followed here.
The validation status. error draws the danger border on the track at every interaction state; default is neutral. Set by the host row and followed here.
Required only for a genuinely standalone control with no host row to name it — the Row provides the accessible name, so a nested control must not double-label.

The binary, with defaultChecked for the uncontrolled form — native naming. onChange is expected to apply the effect immediately: that expectation is the component's contract, and a switch whose change is committed by a later Save button is a Checkbox.Row. For an async effect the controlled value is the server-confirmed source of truth with optimistic local state layered over it.

Rich content, and part of the hit target — the Checkbox.Row label model, inherited. Names the setting as a stable noun or adjective phrase in sentence case ("Airplane mode"), never the state ("Airplane mode is on") and never an action ("Turn on airplane mode"). It does not change on toggle: a label that flips Enable/Disable is disorienting and is a common bug.
Helper beneath the label, describedby-wired. Where the consequence of the setting goes — what turning it on will actually do.

Where Switch.Row differs structurally from Checkbox.Row and Radio.Row, whose control always leads. Defaults to label-leading because a switch's habitat is the settings row, with the toggle at the row's trailing edge where the eye expects it; flip to control-leading when a switch sits inline among other form controls. A prop and not a variants axis: it changes a row's direction and no ink at any coordinate, so it is an anatomy concern (see the header).

Native disabled: removed from the tab order, not submitted, contrast-exempt. Disables the whole row: the nested switch takes its disabled skin and the label dims. Reserve for a setting that does not apply in the current state.

A first-class state here, because an immediate change can still wait on the network. Locks input, swaps the thumb for a spinner and announces aria-busy. The practice ships optimistic-by-default — flip instantly, revert and message on failure — with this as the alternative for high-latency or critical toggles where an inconsistent intermediate is genuinely harmful.

Supported, which is not obvious for a toggle. Enterprise dashboards need users to review permission sets and system config they lack authority to change, and disabling those drops them from the tab order while swapping to static text hides the setting from screen readers. So: aria-readonly="true", focusable and in the tab order, at full WCAG contrast (unlike disabled), and visually distinct from disabled.

The on/off affordance — a checkmark in the thumb when on, an X when off. On by default; turn it off where thumb position plus track color are enough. Never the sole state signal. Exposed from the nested Switch.Control, which carries the glyph. This is not hardcoded "On"/"Off" text adjacent to the label, which is rejected outright: it competes with the track, duplicates the screen-reader output, and does not localize.
The outcome status. error draws the danger border on the track when a change did not take and the thumb reverted; pair it with a status message that says so. default is neutral.

Two rungs, not three: switches rarely warrant a large. Scales the row: the label-to-control gap, the row's minimum height, the label's type, and — passed through to the nested control by follow — the track's height and length and the thumb's diameter.
The visible, persistent label, rendered as the nested FieldLabel. Required — a select always carries a programmatic name. Never the placeholder.

The displayed text — the selected option's label, or the placeholder when nothing is chosen. Controlled: pair with onChange. When it holds the placeholder the ink is the muted placeholder role; a chosen value shows the full-contrast value ink — the same empty-vs-value polarity text-field uses. This is an internal, content-driven distinction, not a variant a designer picks.

The null state shown before a choice is made — plainly the thing to choose ("Country"), not an instruction ("Select a country from the list"), and omittable when the label suffices. Muted, and never load-bearing — it is not the label, not a real option, and it vanishes once a value is chosen.

The bounded set of choices. The select band is roughly 5–15 familiar options: at 4–5 or fewer an always-visible Radio.Group reads better, and past about 15 a filtering combobox (not built yet) scans better.
Fires with the newly chosen value (also onBlur / onFocus). A controlled value with no onChange is read-only by accident.
Persistent guidance, rendered as the nested FieldMessage in its default status; wired via aria-describedby. Show the constraint before failure.

The validation state. Each non-default status swaps the control border to its own boundary (border-only — error → danger, warning → warning, success → success) and sets the nested message to the matching status; default is neutral. The values align with FieldMessage's status axis, so this drives the nested message directly.
The validation text shown at error / warning / success. For error, say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3), never "Invalid".

Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message below the control. Never hides a message the field needs: an error still sets aria-invalid and the message carries the reason, so turn it on wherever there is something to say.
An optional leading glyph before the value (a category or status mark), aria-hidden. Hidden by default; the file nominates the swap target. Signals the field's purpose; validation never mutates it.
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker.
Native disabled — removed from tab order, not submitted, contrast-exempt. Reserve for a choice irrelevant in the current state.

Distinct from disabled: focusable, submitted with the form, and at full contrast, with the value shown and not changeable. Native <select> has no readonly attribute, only disabled, so a read-only select is the custom control with aria-readonly, or a hidden input mirroring the value beside a non-interactive display.
Async options are loading — a spinner replaces the chevron and the control sets aria-busy. Not an empty state: the option list is still arriving. The same name Button and TextField use.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted, tying the label to the control and stitching the aria-describedby chain to the message.
A real control name so the field works uncontrolled, in a native form, and with Server Actions.

Three tiers that scale the value type with the field (small 14px, medium 16px, large 18px, from type.body.sm, md and lg), the nested label one step below it (12 / 14 / 16), and the padding. Every size keeps the 44px target: small is smaller type and padding, not a smaller target; large is taller. small is for fine pointers only: on a coarse pointer (@media (pointer: coarse)) the code sets the small control to 16px, because iOS Safari zooms the page when it focuses a control under 16px. The same prop, with the same values, as TextField and Textarea.

The wash's polarity — a dark wash to lift light text off the image, a light wash to lift dark text. The designer picks it per image from what the photo needs; there is no automatic choice, because which polarity a given photograph wants is a judgment about that image.

How much the wash mutes the image, weakest to strongest. A magnitude, not a contrast promise — a stronger wash darkens (or lightens) the photo more, and whether the text on top clears its floor depends on the image, so verify contrast against your own photo. subtle keeps the image most present; strong mutes it most.

Where the wash sits. full is a solid wash over the whole image. from-top, from-bottom, from-left and from-right put the full intensity at that edge and fade linearly to clear at the opposite edge — for text that sits along one edge. The intensity applies at the named edge only, so verify contrast where the text actually sits.

The width-to-height proportion the frame holds while its actual size flexes — portrait (2:3, 3:4 for apparel tiles, 4:5), a square (1:1), or landscape (the classic photo ratio 4:3, 3:2, widescreen 16:9). It is an aspect-ratio lock, not a pair of fixed dimensions: the frame derives its height from its width (or the reverse) so the shape survives being resized. Pick it from the media the frame will hold.
The icon ladder: 16 / 20 / 24 / 32. The band scales with it (2px at 24). Inside a host slot, take the slot's own icon size.

The accessible name of the spinner's role="status" wrapper, visually hidden and announced politely. "Loading" by default; name the work when it is known ("Loading results"). A host that already announces its own busy state (a Button or IconButton isPending, which set aria-busy and carry their own live region) puts aria-hidden="true" on the spinner instead, so the state is announced once.

Which kind of badge. status = a short label in flow that announces its own text. count = a number over a host, hidden from assistive technology. dot = a contentless mark over a host, also hidden. For a count or dot, the host carries the meaning in its accessible name.

How a status label is drawn. contained = a filled label with padding, in the chosen emphasis. inline = a dot and plain text on the text line, as tall as the line, for running text, list rows and cards. A count and a dot are always contained.

The status label's size. medium = 12px text, about 30px tall, when contained; 16px text on a 24px line when inline. small = 11px text, about 19px tall, when contained; 14px text on a 21px line when inline, for dense layouts such as a label on a product card. A count and a dot come in medium only.

How a status label reads. subtle = the tone's tint with a 1px edge in the tone's border color, for a state that sits beside other content. bold = the solid tone fill, for a state that needs to stand out. surface = the page color with the tone's text and no edge, for a label on a photo or any busy ground, where it brings its own background. A count and a dot are always bold.
Which semantic role the badge paints from. The text carries the meaning, so a tone never stands in for it.
The status text, for type status. One or two words when contained; inline, it can name the whole state. Consistent casing across the product.
The count, for type count. Above max it shows as max followed by a plus sign, formatted for the locale.
The largest count shown in full, for type count. A larger value shows as "99+".
Whether a count of zero still shows, for type count. Hidden by default, since zero is usually nothing to act on.
The host shape a count or dot sits over. circular pulls the badge in toward the curve so it stays on the host's edge, such as an avatar.
The tag text. One word where possible, two or three for a specific entity such as a name or an email address. A long label wraps; it is never cut off.

Which interaction the tag carries. select = toggles on and off, and shows its selected state. dismissible = carries a remove control and has no selected state. This is the component's own prop, not the HTML type attribute, and it is never passed to the element.
Whether a select tag is on. A selected tag takes a tint and a 2px outline, and shows a check mark unless showCheck is off, so the state never rests on color alone. Ignored on a dismissible tag.
Whether a selected select tag shows its check mark after the label. On by default. With it off, the tint and the 2px outline carry the selected state.
The toggle a select tag fires. Suppressed while disabled or read-only.
Called when a dismissible tag's remove control is pressed, or when Delete or Backspace is pressed on the focused tag.
An icon or avatar before the label, for recognition at a glance. Decorative: the label carries the name.

Tag height, padding and label type. Under Tag style Pill the height is Button's: medium clears 44px on comfortable and spacious density, and is 36px at compact. Under Underline the tag hugs its content: 20px, 26px and 32px tall. Under Pill a tag is never narrower than 1.5 times its height, rounded to the nearest 8px (64px for a medium tag on comfortable density); under Underline it has no minimum width.
Removes the tag from interaction and dims it. Don't disable every tag in a group; hide the group instead.
Keeps full visual weight but accepts no interaction, such as a filter the user cannot change. Distinct from disabled, which dims.
The tab text: a short noun, one or two words. One line; a tab list that runs out of room scrolls rather than wrapping.
The key that ties this tab to its panel. The tab list selects by key, never by position.
Whether this tab is the selected one. Set by the tab list from its value; do not set it on a tab inside a list.
An icon before the label. Decorative when a label is present.
A count after the label, drawn as a count badge and read as part of the tab name, such as "Reviews, 12".
Tab height, padding and label type. Medium clears 44px on comfortable and spacious density.
Dims the tab and skips it during arrow-key movement.
The key of the selected tab. Controlled; pair it with onChange.
The tabs, each a Tab, in order, one per panel. Three by default with the first selected, six at most.
The key of the tab selected first, when the list manages its own state.
Called with the new key when the selected tab changes.
automatic: moving focus with the arrow keys selects the tab. manual: arrows move focus only, and Enter or Space selects. Use manual when showing a panel is slow.
The accessible name of the tab list, when nothing on the page already names it.
Passed to every tab.
start: the tabs sit at the start of the bar. center: the tabs sit centered in the bar, which spans its container; the baseline spans the full width either way.

Which way the rule runs. horizontal spans the width of its container and separates content stacked above and below it; vertical spans the height of its container and separates items side by side. A vertical rule sets aria-orientation="vertical"; horizontal is the default and needs no attribute.

How far the rule sits in from its container's edges. none runs edge to edge; inset starts the rule 16px in from the start edge, so it lines up with indented content such as list text after an avatar; middle-inset indents both ends. The start edge follows text direction. A vertical rule takes none or middle-inset only.

How strongly the rule reads. bold (the default) draws it in border.secondary; subtle draws it in border.primary, the lighter border color, for a break that should recede. Both are decorative strengths: a rule that marks a real break sets decorative to false instead.

Whether the rule is only visual. true (the default) hides it from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true". Set false when the rule marks a real break in the content: it becomes a separator, an <hr> for a horizontal rule, drawn in border.tertiary so it reaches 3:1 on every background. It has no effect on a labeled divider, where the label marks the break.

One short word that breaks the rule in the middle, such as Or. Setting it makes a labeled divider: a line on each side, centered on the label. No inset only. A vertical labeled divider keeps the label upright, with a line above and below it. Screen readers read the label as plain text and skip the two lines. Pass the translated word.
Which pair of glyphs shows: a chevron (down closed, up open) or a plus and minus (plus closed, minus open).
Whether the section the glyph belongs to is open. Set by the Accordion it sits in.
The glyph size. Set by the Accordion it sits in.
The header text: a short noun phrase, or a question in an FAQ, that tells the user what the panel holds. It wraps rather than truncating.
The panel content. Hidden from the page, the tab order and assistive technology while the section is closed.
The key a group of accordions uses to track which sections are open. A stable key is safer than a position when sections are added or reordered.
Opens the section on first render when nothing controls it.
The level of the heading that wraps the header button. Set it one below the heading the accordion sits under, so the page outline stays intact.
The open and closed glyph: a chevron that points down when closed and up when open, or a plus that becomes a minus.
Which side of the title the indicator sits on, following text direction. leading keeps it beside the title when the page is zoomed; in right-to-left text, leading is the right edge.
Shows the divider under the section. Turn it off when the design separates sections another way, such as spacing, a card or a background, so the page does not draw two separators.
The header's type, padding and indicator size. Every size keeps the header at least 44px tall.

The item text: a short phrase or sentence. It wraps under itself. Inline content such as a link is allowed; a block such as a second list is a nested list, indented by this item's marker column, so it starts at this item's text edge.
Which marker the item shows. Set by the List from its own type; do not set it on an item inside a List.
The text size, 12, 14, 16 or 18px, and the marker sized to it. Set by the List.
In an ordered list, the number this item shows; the items after it count on from it. Leave it unset to let the list count.
The marker glyph when type is icon. A check by default. Decorative: the item text carries the meaning.

unordered (a <ul> with bullets) when the order carries no meaning; ordered (an <ol>, numbered) when it does; icon (a <ul> with an icon before each item) for points such as requirements or features. Passed to every item.
The text size, 12, 14, 16 or 18px, with the marker, the marker column and the space between items sized to it. Use x-small for tight rule lists, such as password requirements. Passed to every item.
Ordered only: the number the first item shows.
Ordered only: count down instead of up.
The items, each a List.Item, in order. Three by default; a designer adds, removes and reorders them in place.
The option name: a short noun or noun phrase, one line.
The value the control reports when this option is selected.
Whether this option is the selected one. Set by the control from its value; do not set it on an option inside a control.
An icon before the label. Decorative when a label is shown.
Option height, padding and label type. Passed down by the control.
Dims this one option and takes it out of interaction, while the rest of the control stays usable.
What is being chosen, such as "View". Shown above the track, or given as an accessible name only when the page already shows it.
The options, each a SegmentedControl.Segment, in order. Three by default with the first selected, five at most.
The selected option's value. Controlled; pair it with onChange.
The option selected first, when the control manages its own state. A segmented control always has one option selected.
Called with the new value when the selection changes. Never called with an empty value.

view: a group of buttons that changes the current view at once, the selected one marked as current. form: a radio group whose value is submitted with a form. One look, two behaviors; never wire one as the other.
Passed to every option. Medium is a button's height, 44px on comfortable and spacious density.
auto: every option as wide as the widest. full: the control fills its column and the options share it equally.
The form field name, in the form behavior.
Disables every option and takes the control out of the Tab order.
The link text. It names the destination and makes sense read on its own, without the sentence around it.
The destination: a URL, a fragment such as "#main", or a file. With no href, render plain text rather than a link.
Standalone shows its underline at hover, pressed and focus; inline is underlined at every state, for a link in body copy.
Emphasis is the starting value; choose Default for a lighter weight link.
The body type size: 12, 14, 16 or 18px. The box is one text line tall; the icon (16px at x-small, small and medium, 20px at large) sits inside it.
Marks the link to the page the user is on, in a navigation: a 2px bar under the text and aria-current="page". Standalone links only. It stays a link with its href.
The ground the link sits on: the page, or a dark or brand-filled band, which takes the inverse link colors.
Opens in a new tab: adds the trailing external icon, visually hidden "(opens in new tab)" text and rel="noopener noreferrer". Keep it for narrow cases.
Merges the link's styling and accessibility onto a router's link child, so one anchor renders and the component depends on no router.
An icon after the label, such as an arrow or the external icon. Not for inline links.
The buttons, each a Button, Button.Destructive or Button.Neutral, in order. Two by default, three at most. Inline and fill, the main action last; stacked, the main action first.

inline is a row at the end edge; stacked is a column of full-width buttons, the main action on top; fill is a row whose buttons share the width. A row too wide for its space wraps; nothing switches layout by itself.
Whether the dialog is showing. Opening it moves focus into it and makes the page behind it inert.
Called with false on every attempt to close: the close button, Escape, a backdrop click on a standard dialog, or an action that closes it. Keep open in step with it.
The heading that names the task. It is the dialog's accessible name, so make it specific: "Delete this address?", not "Are you sure?". It wraps rather than truncating.
One or two sentences under the title that say what the dialog is for or what an action will do. Linked as the dialog's accessible description.
The body content. The body is the only part that scrolls; the header and footer stay in place.

The footer buttons, one to three Button elements, laid out by a Button group. Inline and fill, the main action last (Cancel, then Save); stacked, the main action first. Fill suits two. Name each by what it does.

dialog for a task or form. alertdialog for a confirmation that interrupts and needs an answer: it hides the close button, a backdrop click does not close it, and focus starts on the least destructive action.

Where the panel sits. center on every screen by default; bottom (a bottom sheet) and full (full screen) are for small screens; end (a side sheet) runs the full height of the screen at the end edge, the right in left-to-right text. Set per breakpoint; nothing switches automatically.

The width of a centered panel: 400, 560 or 720px. On a small screen a centered panel is as wide as the screen less its margins. Bottom and full panels are full width, and an end panel is 480px wide, so all three ignore it.

How the actions are laid out. inline is a row at the end edge; stacked is full-width buttons, the main action on top; fill is a row whose buttons share the width equally, the main action last; none is for a dialog whose body holds its own actions.
The visible, persistent label (rendered as FieldLabel), usually "Password" or "New password". Required. Never the placeholder.
Controlled value; pair with onChange.
Uncontrolled initial value.
Change handler (also onBlur / onFocus).
An example only; vanishes on input. The password rules belong in helper text or a list under the field, never here.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage, default status), wired via aria-describedby. State the rules for a new password here, before the user types.

The validation state, as on TextField: each non-default status swaps the input border and sets the nested message to the matching status; error also sets aria-invalid. The Show/Hide button never takes the status color.
The validation text shown at error / warning / success, added to aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3).
Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message. Never hides a message the field needs.
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker.
Native disabled. Disables the Show/Hide button with the field.
Focusable, copyable and submitted, and passes contrast. The Show/Hide button stays live, so a read-only value can still be shown.
Required (SC 1.3.5): current-password on a sign-in form, new-password where the user sets one, so a password manager fills or offers to generate it. Never off.
An optional leading glyph before the value, aria-hidden and never the accessible name. Hidden by default; the file nominates the swap target.
Async validation in progress; sets aria-busy; does not block typing.

TextField's three tiers: the input type and the nested label scale with it. The Show/Hide button is small at every size, so the label row stays one label line tall. Every size keeps the input's 44px target; the button's hit area is 44×44 at medium and large and 24×24 at small, in code.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted. The Show/Hide button's aria-controls names it.
A real <input name>, so the field works in a native <form> and a password manager recognizes it.
The status, a few words stating the outcome ("Added to bag"). It wraps onto a second line rather than truncating.
neutral for a plain confirmation, with no glyph. success adds a circled check beside the message. A message the user must not miss, such as an error, is a banner, not a toast.
At most one action, a text button named by one verb ("Undo", "View bag"). The same action must also exist elsewhere on the page. A toast with an action does not close by itself.
How long a toast with no action shows, in milliseconds. Never less than 5000; a shorter value is raised to 5000. Raise it for a longer or translated message. Ignored when there is an action.
Shows the close button, named "Dismiss". On by default: it is the one exit a user can count on.
Called when the toast closes for any reason: the close button, the timer, the next toast replacing it, or the action.
chevron: a chevron pointing toward the current page. slash: a forward slash. Set by the Breadcrumbs it sits in, for every step at once.

ancestor: a link to a page above this one. current: the page you are on, as text. overflow: the button that stands for the hidden steps of a long trail. Breadcrumbs sets it from the item's place in the trail.
The page name, as the page titles itself. On an ancestor it is the link text; on the current page, the text.
The ancestor page's address. Ignored on the current page, which is not a link.
The body type size, 14 or 16px, with the gap to the separator sized to it. Set by the Breadcrumbs it sits in.
The mark after the step: a chevron or a slash. Set by the Breadcrumbs it sits in, the same for every step. Unused on the current page.
The steps, root first, each with a label and an href. The last is rendered as the current page: text with aria-current="page", its href ignored. At least two.
The body type size, 14 or 16px, passed to every item. Medium suits a trail beside 16px body copy; small, a quieter line above a page title.
The mark between steps, the same for every step: a chevron pointing toward the current page, or a slash.
Above this many items, the middle collapses behind one overflow button.
How many items stay before the overflow button when the trail collapses.
How many items stay after the overflow button: the parent and the current page by default.
What the overflow button does: expand shows the hidden steps in place and moves focus to the first of them.
Below 480px, show one link up to the parent page in place of the trail. Turn it off where the full trail fits.
The accessible name of the navigation landmark, translated. Assistive technology adds "navigation" itself.
Renders each ancestor through a router's link, so one anchor renders and the component depends on no router. The plain anchor by default.
What is counted, such as "Quantity". The accessible name of the value, always present in code; shown above the counter only with showLabel.
Shows the label above the counter. Off by default: a counter on a product card or a bag line is usually explained by what sits around it, and the label stays its accessible name either way.
Controlled value; pair it with onChange.
The starting value when the counter manages its own state. Defaults to min.
Called with the new number after each step. Never called with a value outside min and max.
The lowest value. At min, the minus button is unavailable.
The highest value, such as the stock or a per-order limit. At max, the plus button is unavailable. No max means no upper limit.
How much one press or one arrow key changes the value.
outline draws the field edge around the row, with the minus and plus glyphs inside it. ghost draws no box, and the minus and plus are light circles at each end.
The row height (36, 44 or 56px), the value type (14, 16 or 18px) and the glyph (20, 20 or 24px). Each button keeps a hit area of at least 44×44px in code at every size.
Text below the counter, such as the reason for a limit ("Limit 5 per order"). Added to the value's description.
Shows the message below the counter. Off by default.
The minus button's accessible name. Defaults to "Decrease" followed by the label, such as "Decrease quantity". In a list of line items, include the item: "Decrease quantity, Trail runner".
The plus button's accessible name. Defaults to "Increase" followed by the label. In a list of line items, include the item.
The form field name: a hidden input carries the value when the counter sits in a form.
Disables the whole counter: the value leaves the Tab order and both buttons are unavailable.
The page number as shown, such as "4". Pagination sets it, through the locale's number format.
The page this cell opens. Absent on an ellipsis.
The address of the page. Present, the cell is a link; absent, it is a button that changes the page in place.
Whether this is the current page. Set by Pagination; do not set it on a cell inside a pagination row.

page: a page number the user can open. ellipsis: the three-dot icon that stands for two or more pages not shown. previous and next: the cell with a left or right chevron that opens the page before or after the current one.
On previous and next only: true shows the word beside the chevron, as Pagination's simple type does. Passed down by Pagination.
The word a labeled previous cell shows, "Previous" by default. Pass the translated word.
The word a labeled next cell shows, "Next" by default. Pass the translated word.
On previous and next only: true at the first or last page. The cell stays in place and in the Tab order with aria-disabled="true", and does nothing when activated. Set by Pagination.
How the current page is marked: a border around the cell, or a 2px line under the number. Passed down by Pagination.
The cell height and label type, matching the icon buttons beside it. Passed down by Pagination.
The total number of pages. Pagination is not shown when it is 1.
The current page, counted from 1. Controlled; pair it with onPageChange.
The page shown first, when Pagination manages its own state.
Called with the new page number when the user opens a page.

Returns the address of a page. Present, every page is a link the user can bookmark, share or open in a new tab; absent, every page is a button that changes the content in place. Pass it whenever the page has an address.
Renders a page as your router's link, keeping its address and aria-current.

numbered: page numbers between previous and next. compact: "Page 5 of 10" between previous and next. simple: Previous and Next only. A numbered row switches to compact when its container is narrower than the row.
How the current page is marked in a numbered row: a border around it, or a 2px line under its number.
The size of every cell and button, matching the icon button sizes. Medium is 44px on comfortable and spacious density.
How many pages show on each side of the current page.
How many pages show at each end.
The accessible name of the navigation landmark. Give two pagination rows on one page the same name, or a name each ("Pagination, top").
Returns the compact text and the page-change announcement, "Page 5 of 10" by default. Pass a translated string with the page and the count in the order the language needs.

determinate = the work can be measured, so the bar shows how far it has got. indeterminate = it cannot, so a segment sweeps along the track and there is no value. Choose indeterminate rather than faking a value.

How far the work has got, between min and max, for a determinate bar. Omitted, the bar rests at min. Out-of-range values are clamped, with a warning in development. Never fake a value: a bar that creeps toward the end and stops there breaks the contract. If the work cannot be measured, set type to indeterminate.
The start of the range.
The end of the range: 100 for a percentage, or the total, such as a byte count.
What is in progress, with an active verb ("Uploading photo.jpg"). It is the accessible name. A linear bar shows it above the track; a ring is named by it without showing it.
The visible value, and the same string as aria-valuetext. A percentage by default, through Intl.NumberFormat, so "45%" localizes. Prefer a concrete amount when there is one ("45 MB of 100 MB").
linear = a bar that fills its container. circular = a ring for a small space, determinate or indeterminate. An indeterminate ring shows no value.
The ring's size: medium is 40px with a 4px band, small is 24px with a 3px band. A linear bar has one thickness, 4px, and ignores this.

active = the work is running. complete = it finished: the fill turns to the success color and the message names the result. error = it failed: the fill stops where it failed, turns to the danger color, and the message names the problem and the next step.

The outcome, shown below the bar at complete and error with a glyph: past tense when done ("Upload complete"), the problem and the next step when it fails ("Upload failed. The connection dropped. Try again.").
Whether the value text shows. On by default. A ring keeps it on: it has no end to mark, so the value is how the amount reads.

What a screen reader hears. milestones = once as the value passes 25, 50 and 75%, and again at the end. end = the end only. none = the host announces the work itself. An error is announced when it happens, except under none.
Milliseconds to wait before showing the bar. If the work finishes first, nothing shows, so a fast task does not flash a bar.
Milliseconds the bar stays once shown, so it does not vanish after one frame.
The persistent label (rendered as FieldLabel), usually "Search" or what is searched ("Search products"). Required, even when hidden. Never the placeholder.
Hides the label visually and keeps it in the accessibility tree, so the field keeps its name. For a search whose purpose is plain from where it sits, such as a site header. Never display: none.
Controlled value; pair with onChange.
Uncontrolled initial value.
Change handler (also onBlur / onFocus). Also fires with an empty value when the clear button clears the field.
An example query only; vanishes on input. Never the label.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage, default status), wired via aria-describedby. Off by default in most searches.

The validation state, as on TextField: each non-default status swaps the input border and sets the nested message to the matching status; error also sets aria-invalid. A search rarely needs one; a query that is too short is one case.
The validation text shown at error / warning / success, added to aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it (SC 3.3.3).

Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message below the input. Never hides a message the field needs: turn it on wherever there is helper or validation text.
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker.
Native disabled. The clear button is not shown while the field is disabled.
Focusable, copyable and submitted, and passes contrast. The clear button is not shown, because the value cannot change.
Usually off for a site search, so the browser does not offer earlier queries over the page. Pass a token where a saved value helps.
The search glyph before the value, aria-hidden and never the accessible name. Shown by default; turn it off or swap it where the field's purpose needs a different mark.

The clear button's glyph, close-filled by default. In code the clear button is a focusable button named "Clear search", shown only while the field holds a value. Its hit area is at least 24×24 px, drawn around the 20px glyph, and adds no height to the field.
Called after the clear button empties the field, with focus back on the input.
Results are loading; sets aria-busy and does not block typing.

TextField's three tiers: the input type, the nested label and the padding scale with it. Every size keeps the 44px target. small is for fine pointers only: on a coarse pointer the code sets the small input to 16px, because iOS Safari zooms the page when it focuses an input under 16px. The edge, outline or underline, is the brand's Search field style setting, not a prop.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted. The clear button's aria-controls names it.
A real <input name>, so the query submits with the host's form ("q" is common).
The visible, persistent label (rendered as FieldLabel), usually "Card number". Required. Never the placeholder.
Controlled value: the digits only, without the spaces the field shows between groups. Pair with onChange.
Uncontrolled initial value, digits only.
Change handler (also onBlur / onFocus). Receives the digits without the group spaces.
A format example only, such as "1234 1234 1234 1234". It vanishes on input and never replaces the label.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage, default status), wired via aria-describedby, such as "The card type shows when you start typing."

The validation state, as on TextField: each non-default status swaps the input border and sets the nested message to the matching status; error also sets aria-invalid. A number that fails the checksum is a warning, not an error, because some valid cards fail it. The tile never takes the status color.
The validation text shown at error / warning / success, added to aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it, such as "Enter the card number."
Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to render the helper or validation message. Never hides a message the field needs.
Sets required / aria-required, and turns on the FieldLabel's required marker.
Native disabled. A disabled field also disables a hosted input. The tile keeps its own colors.
Focusable, copyable and submitted, and passes contrast, as on TextField. For a saved card, show the last four digits in a read-only display instead of this field.

The card network the field shows: generic until the leading digits tell the network, then that network's tile. Set it from the card-type detection, or from the payment provider's card-brand event when the provider hosts the input. Card networks only: a wallet or pay-later tile is never a value, because no card number names one.

The detected network's name in the app's own words, such as "Visa". It goes in a visually hidden description on the input, linked by aria-describedby, so the network is never conveyed by the tile alone. Leave it empty while brand is generic.
Whether the tile shows. On by default; the field shows the generic tile before it knows the network.

Returns the payment provider's mount point, the element its hosted input mounts into. With it, the field draws the label, box, tile, focus edge and message around the provider's input and never renders the card number input itself. Without it, the field renders a native input, which puts the page outside the lightest card-data compliance scope.
Async validation in progress; sets aria-busy; does not block typing.
An optional leading glyph before the value, aria-hidden and never the accessible name. Hidden by default; the file nominates the swap target.

TextField's three tiers: the input type and the nested label scale with it. The tile is 20px tall at small and medium and 24px at large, its width from the tile's proportion. Every size keeps the input's 44px target.
Wiring + form submission; auto-generated with useId if omitted, tying label to input and the aria-describedby chain.
A real <input name> in the native mode, so the field works in a native <form>. A hosted input has no name on the page.

How serious the message is. Sets the fill, the edge and the glyph. Match it to the message: danger for an error that blocks the user, warning for a risk, success for a finished process, info for other status news, and neutral for a message with no status, such as an announcement or a membership offer. Neutral sits on the secondary background with a neutral edge and shows no glyph.

contained is a rounded box with an edge on all four sides, inside a section or card. full-bleed is a bar across the top of the page, for a message about the whole app: square corners, and an edge on the top and bottom only, so it runs edge to edge.
A short heading that names the issue ("Payment failed"), with no period at the end. When present, it labels the banner's region.
The body: what happened and what to do next, in one or two sentences. Usually plain text; it can hold a short list or other rich content instead. Never repeat the title.
The heading level of the title, matched to where the banner sits in the page outline, so the outline stays in order.
Replaces the tone glyph, or false to hide it in a dense layout. The glyph is hidden from assistive technology either way.

One text Button that resolves the message (Button.Neutral when the file has it), under the body. Name it by what it does ("Retry", "Update billing"). A banner carries one action at most, so a banner with actions takes no link.

com.prism3.type: { label: string; href: string }, never with actions
com.prism3.description: A link at the end of the body sentence, for a one-line message whose action goes somewhere ("Faster checkout by becoming a member. Join"). It renders as an inline Link, underlined, appended to the body paragraph, and wraps under the text when the line has no room. A banner carries one action at most, so a banner with a link takes no actions. Name the outcome where it fits ("Become a member").
Whether the banner shows a dismiss button. Set it together with onDismiss. Leave a banner about a condition that still blocks the user not dismissible.
Called when the dismiss button is pressed. Remove the banner, store the dismissal so it does not return on reload, and move focus to a sensible place.

Whether a banner inserted after the page loads is announced: auto announces it through the page's live region, assertively for danger and politely otherwise. A banner present when the page loads is never announced; it is read in order.
The thumb's accessible name. Set by the Slider: the label for a single value, "Minimum {label}" and "Maximum {label}" for a range.
The disc's diameter: 18, 24 or 30px at the default density, from control.size.*.thumb. Set by the Slider.
The disabled look. Set by the Slider when the whole control is disabled.
Names the dimension being set, such as "Price" or "Volume". Shown above the track, and the accessible name of a single thumb.
The value. A number sets one thumb; a pair of numbers, such as [40, 120], sets a range with two thumbs. Controlled; pair it with onChange.
The starting value when the slider manages its own state. A pair starts a range.
Called on every change while dragging or stepping, for a live preview.
Called once when the pointer is released or a key step ends. Bind costly work here, such as a network filter, so a drag does not call it for every pixel.
The lowest value.
The highest value.
The amount one arrow key or one snap moves. Every value is rounded to the nearest exact multiple of the step before onChange.
The amount Page Up and Page Down move. Ten steps when not set.
For a range, how many steps the two thumbs must stay apart. A thumb stops there and never crosses the other.
How the value reads: a currency, a percent, a unit. Drives the visible value text and each thumb's aria-valuetext from one formatter, so what is seen and what is heard match.
For a range, the two thumb names. "Minimum {label}" and "Maximum {label}" when not set.
Read from value: a number is single, a pair is range. Not set on its own; listed so the two looks have a name.
The thumb and the track: an 18px thumb on a 2px track, 24 on 4, or 30 on 6. The label, the value text and the 44px hit area stay the same at every size.
Shows the value text above the track. Turn it off only when the paired inputs show the value instead.
Shows labeled milestones under the track: the minimum and the maximum at its ends, and any values in milestones between them, each under its own position.

The values labeled under the track when showMilestones is on, such as [500, 1000]. A plain number is formatted like the value text; an object gives its own label. The minimum and the maximum are always labeled.
Shows paired number inputs under the track: one for a single value, "Minimum" and "Maximum" for a range. Typing moves the thumb; dragging updates the input. With inputs on, turn the value text off.
Guidance under the slider, in a field message.

error marks the slider invalid: the field message shows the error status and each thumb carries aria-invalid. A slider's own value is always in range, so an error comes from a paired input or from validation elsewhere in the form.
The error text, shown in the field message and added to aria-describedby. Say what is wrong and how to fix it.
Takes the slider out of interaction and out of the form payload, and dims it.
The thumbs stay focusable and the value is still submitted, but it cannot change. Looks like rest.
The form field name. A range submits two values.
The character this cell shows: one digit, or one letter in a code that allows letters. Empty until the user reaches it.
The cell size and its character size. Set by the code input.
Whether this is the cell the next character goes into while the input has focus. Set by the code input.
Whether the code input is in error. Set by the code input.
Whether the code input is disabled. Set by the code input.
The visible label (rendered as FieldLabel), such as "Verification code". Required.
How many characters the code has, 4 to 8. Draws that many cells and caps the value at that length.
Controlled value; pair with onChange.
Uncontrolled initial value.
Called with the value after spaces and hyphens are removed.
Called once with the value when it reaches the set length, and again only if the value changes and reaches it again. The page decides whether to submit.
numeric for a code of digits, text for a code with letters.
one-time-code by default, so the phone offers the code from the message. Never off.
Persistent guidance (rendered as FieldMessage): how many characters and where the code was sent.
error swaps every cell to the danger border, sets the message to the error status and sets aria-invalid.
The error text: too few characters, a wrong code or an expired code, each said plainly.

Whether the composed FieldMessage is shown. Off by default; turn it on to show the helper or validation message below the cells. Never hides a message the field needs: turn it on wherever there is helper or validation text.
The cell size: small 44×44 with a 16px character, medium 48×56 with 20px, large 56×64 with 24px, xlarge 68×72 with 40px, meant for four-character codes.
auto: each cell at its size. full: the row spans its container and the cells share it, shrinking to 32px wide when they must.
Native disabled.
The code is being checked; sets aria-busy and keeps the input editable.
A real <input name>, so the field works in a native <form>.
Wiring; generated if omitted.
